quoted_clause: the MoE challenger from Ch 3 was rejected on total-weight residency and compute grounds: MoE total parameters exceed the dense 70B, so the 140 GB weight floor grows, and expert dispatch adds overhead
observed: The clause uses total parameter count to justify a compute rejection. Total parameters determine weight residency, not per-token compute; MoE compute depends on active parameters and routing. A MoE with total params >70B can have active params <70B and lower per-token FLOPs, while adding dispatch/communication overhead.
evidence: Standard MoE arithmetic: per-token FLOPs scale with active parameters, not total parameters; memory residency scales with total parameters. The clause conflates the two and does not provide measured active-param compute or dispatch cost.
root_cause: Conflation of memory residency with compute cost; missing active-parameter distinction.
correction: Rewrite to separate: (a) total-weight residency may exceed 140 GB, increasing HBM pressure; (b) per-token compute depends on active parameters and may be lower or higher; (c) expert dispatch adds communication/overhead. Reject MoE only after comparing measured active-param compute, dispatch overhead, and residency against the SLO. If Ch 3 already establishes this, cite it and avoid the total-params-to-compute inference.
acceptance_test: The revised paragraph must not infer compute cost from total parameter count; it must state active-parameter compute and dispatch overhead as separate criteria, with a measured or clearly labeled illustrative comparison.

quoted_clause: for a Llama-style 70B model, n_layers = 80, d_model = 8192, bytes per element = 2 (FP16). KV cache per token = n_layers × 2 × d_model × bytes = 80 ×2 × 8192 ×2 = 2,621,440 bytes ≈ 2.62 MB/token
observed: The formula assumes full multi-head attention (all d_model dimensions have K/V per layer). Actual Llama 2 70B uses grouped-query attention with 8 KV heads, so its KV cache is much smaller. Calling the geometry 'Llama-style' while using full-MHA arithmetic can mislead readers into applying 2.62 MB/token to a real Llama 70B checkpoint.
evidence: Llama 2 70B config: 80 layers, hidden 8192, 64 attention heads, 8 KV heads. KV per token = n_layers * 2 * n_kv_heads * head_dim * bytes = 80*2*8*128*2 = 327,680 bytes ≈0.33 MB/token, not 2.62 MB/token. The book's house convention says canonical 70B full-MHA reference, but the text says 'Llama-style' without that qualifier.
root_cause: Terminology drift between canonical full-MHA teaching geometry and real Llama GQA architecture.
correction: Replace 'Llama-style 70B model' with 'canonical full-MHA 70B teaching geometry' and add a parenthetical: 'A real GQA Llama 70B checkpoint would use n_kv_heads < n_heads and a correspondingly smaller KV cache; the full-MHA figure is the book's conservative canonical reference.' Or explicitly state the full-MHA assumption in the formula.
acceptance_test: The paragraph must not call the full-MHA geometry 'Llama-style' without qualification; it must state the full-MHA assumption and note GQA reduces KV by n_heads/n_kv_heads.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b) 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included'
quoted_clause: The 9,000 tokens-per-dollar figure is an output-token metric (50 output tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20); under continuous batching ... on a combined prefill+decode basis the same host moves 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s ≈ 285,000 tokens/$ ...; the single-stream floor is 9,500/7.08 ≈ 1,342 tok/s ≈ 242,000 tokens/$
observed: The 9,000 figure counts output tokens only and ignores prefill time. The 285,000 and 242,000 figures count combined input+output tokens and include prefill time. They are different denominators and token populations, so presenting them in one sequence as if they were comparable can mislead. The 'single-stream floor' 242,000 is not a floor for the 9,000 output-token metric; it is a combined-token metric.
evidence: 9,000 = 50 output tok/s * 3600 / 20. 242,000 = (9,500 tokens/request / 7.08 s) * 3600 / 20. The first is output-only decode rate; the second is combined input+output full-request rate. A full-request output-token metric would be (300/7.08)*3600/20 ≈ 7,627 output tokens/$, not 9,000.
root_cause: Mixing output-token and combined-token denominators in the same economic comparison.
correction: Label each metric explicitly: (a) 9,000 output tokens/$ at decode-only 50 tok/s; (b) ~7,600 output tokens/$ for the single-stream full request including prefill; (c) ~242,000 combined tokens/$ single-stream; (d) ~285,000 combined tokens/$ at the stated batched output rate. Do not call 242,000 a floor for the 9,000 output-token figure.
acceptance_test: The revised passage must state the token population (output-only vs combined) and whether prefill time is included for every tokens/$ figure, and must not compare figures with different denominators as if they were the same metric.

quoted_clause: The decision hinges on whether the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain ... translates into sufficient answer-quality improvement to justify the ~4.8×FLOP cost (14.08 vs 2.94 GFLOP per 64-token query, Table 5-1)
observed: The ~15% MAP prior is introduced as a within-family/controlled-dimension effect. The 4.8× FLOP cost is a cross-model comparison between all-mpnet-base-v2 (768-d, ~110M) and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384-d, ~23M). The text uses a dimension-only prior as if it were the expected quality gain of the cross-model choice.
evidence: The preceding HYPOTHESIS says 'within a given embedding family or a controlled dimensionality experiment' and 'reports range from a few to ~15% MAP difference'. The cost ratio 14.08/2.94 is from Table 5-1 total-parameter proxy, not a dimension-only comparison. The text later admits the quality gain is 'not quantified for this model pair', which contradicts using the 15% prior as the decision hinge.
root_cause: Conflating a dimension-only quality prior with a cross-model quality difference.
correction: Rewrite: 'The cross-model quality gain of all-mpnet over MiniLM is unmeasured; the ~15% MAP prior is a dimension-only upper bound and cannot be assumed to transfer across model families. The decision therefore requires measuring the actual mpnet-vs-MiniLM quality gap on the target corpus before paying the ~4.8× FLOP cost.' Or if a cross-model prior exists, cite it.
acceptance_test: The revised passage must not use the dimension-only ~15% prior as the expected cross-model quality gain; it must state that the cross-model gain is unmeasured and require target-corpus measurement.

page_hint: Ch 5 §3(b) final paragraph of 'tokens/s per dollar with prefill included'
quoted_clause: GPU-hour cost follows occupancy, batching and scheduling — it is not proportional to either share without a stated utilization assumption. The per-dollar economics therefore favor models that reduce the prefill compute burden ... more than models that optimize decode throughput alone
observed: The first sentence denies a fixed proportionality between cost and FLOP share; the next sentence draws a directional cost conclusion from the FLOP share. The 'therefore' does not follow without a stated operating regime (throughput-bound vs latency-bound) and utilization assumption.
evidence: If the deployment is latency-bound by decode, reducing decode time may improve goodput or allow higher batch, even if prefill is 97% of FLOPs. If prefill is the throughput bottleneck at high utilization, prefill reduction may dominate. The text itself says 'a deployment must balance both' and 'decode still sets the latency SLO', which undercuts the unqualified 'favor'.
root_cause: Missing operating-point qualifier; cost conclusion drawn from FLOP share after explicitly saying cost is not proportional to FLOP share.
correction: Qualify: 'Under a throughput-bound, high-utilization regime where prefill FLOPs are the limiting resource, reducing prefill compute can improve tokens/$ more than decode-only optimizations. Under a latency-bound regime, decode optimizations may dominate. The architect must measure the bottleneck and utilization before choosing.' Remove or condition the unqualified 'therefore favor'.
acceptance_test: The revised passage must state the operating regime and utilization assumption under which prefill optimization is favored, and must not infer cost direction from FLOP share alone.

page_hint: Ch 5 §5 Common Mistakes, 'Ignoring the KV cache cost of long contexts'
quoted_clause: hit SLO violations when the cache spills to host memory or SSD
observed: 'Spills' suggests automatic cache-like behavior. Serving engines may preempt, swap, or offload KV blocks, but the mechanism is implementation-specific and not a generic spill. The phrase can mislead readers about how KV capacity pressure manifests.
evidence: PagedAttention/vLLM can preempt sequences and recompute or swap KV blocks; other engines may reject/admit differently. There is no universal 'spill to SSD' behavior.
root_cause: Informal cache terminology applied to KV memory management.
correction: Replace with 'when KV capacity pressure forces preemption, swapping, recomputation, or admission control (depending on the serving engine)'.
acceptance_test: The revised sentence must not imply a universal automatic spill-to-host/SSD behavior; it must name the engine-dependent mechanisms.

page_hint: Ch 5 §7 What We Still Don't Know, first paragraph
quoted_clause: no public study quantifies this domain-dependence
observed: This is a strong negative literature claim. The chapter does not cite a literature search, and embedding-dimension/domain studies may exist. In a HYPOTHESIS paragraph, 'no public study' reads as an asserted fact.
evidence: The manuscript provides no citation or search protocol for the absence claim. The surrounding text already labels the relationship as domain-specific and unverified; the absolute 'no public study' is unnecessary.
root_cause: Overstrong negative claim in an uncertainty section.
correction: Soften to 'we are not aware of a public study that quantifies this domain-dependence for these model families' or 'the public evidence is insufficient to quantify it for this corpus.' If a literature search was performed, cite its scope and date.
acceptance_test: The revised sentence must either cite a search scope/date or be phrased as the authors' awareness/evidence gap, not as an absolute absence of public studies.

quoted_clause: canonical SLO targets are TTFT 1.2 s / TPOT ~25 ms
observed: The chapter states the canonical SLO is TTFT 1.2 s, but later repeatedly uses a 2 s p95 TTFT SLO: 'canonical p95 TTFT SLO of ≤ 2 s', 'with a p95 ≤ 2 s', and the mini-case uses 'a 2 s SLO'. The goodput example also assumes a 2 s threshold.
evidence: These are not compatible as stated: a 1.2 s TTFT SLO and a 2 s p95 TTFT SLO are different operating contracts. The later examples depend on the 2 s value, while the canonical SLO statement depends on 1.2 s.
root_cause: Canonical SLO definition has drifted or is being used at two different scopes (design target vs p95 SLO) without explicit distinction.
correction: Define one canonical SLO contract explicitly: either TTFT p95 ≤ 1.2 s, or TTFT target 1.2 s with p95 SLO ≤ 2 s. Then update every downstream example, table, and mini-case to use that contract consistently.
acceptance_test: Search all occurrences of '1.2 s', '2 s', 'p95 TTFT', and 'SLO' in Chapter 6. Every occurrence must resolve to the same explicitly defined canonical SLO contract, with no example using a different threshold without labeling it as a separate illustrative scenario.

quoted_clause: prefix caching is a partial mitigation (~13% of prefill FLOPs), not the fix
observed: The mini-case later says: 'prefix-cache hit ratio ~13% and the predicted ~13% prefill reduction explain the 2.4 s → <2 s move; goodput restored.' This directly contradicts the earlier statement that prefix caching is not the fix.
evidence: If the system is ~18.6× oversubscribed at the 40 rps peak, a 13% prefill-FLOP reduction leaves it ~16.2× oversubscribed. That cannot by itself bring p95 TTFT from 2.4 s to below 2 s. The mini-case also says the resolution is capacity/scheduling, but then credits prefix caching with the recovery.
root_cause: The mini-case's causal closure is inconsistent: it mixes a partial compute-saving mitigation with a capacity/scheduling fix and then attributes the observed recovery to the partial mitigation.
correction: Rewrite the mini-case so the mechanism check matches the arithmetic. Either (a) state that additional hosts/scheduling were applied and quantify the new capacity, or (b) keep prefix caching as a partial mitigation and show that it alone cannot close an 18.6× gap. Do not claim that a 13% prefill reduction explains a 2.4 s → <2 s recovery under 18.6× oversubscription.
acceptance_test: Recompute the post-mitigation prefill demand and capacity in the mini-case. The stated cause of the p95 TTFT recovery must be quantitatively sufficient to move the system from 2.4 s to below the SLO. If prefix caching is credited, the arithmetic must show that the remaining oversubscription is compatible with the observed latency.

quoted_clause: The architecture is memory- and compute-sane at the 10 rps design point but was never sized for the lunch peak.
observed: The mini-case diagnoses ~18.6× prefill oversubscription at 40 rps using a host capacity of ~2.77 PFLOP/s. At 10 rps, the same arithmetic gives 10 × 1.29 ≈ 12.9 PFLOP/s, which is ~4.66× the stated host capacity. A single host is therefore not compute-sane at 10 rps either.
evidence: 10 rps × 1.29 PFLOP/request = 12.9 PFLOP/s. 12.9 / 2.77 ≈ 4.66. The text's own capacity figure makes the 10 rps design point oversubscribed if only one host is assumed. If multiple hosts are assumed, the 18.6× figure at 40 rps no longer follows from the stated host capacity.
root_cause: The mini-case does not specify the host count consistently. The 18.6× figure assumes one host; the 'sane at 10 rps' claim assumes enough hosts to serve 10 rps. Both cannot be true with the same host count.
correction: Specify the deployed host count in the mini-case. Then recompute both the 10 rps design-point utilization and the 40 rps peak oversubscription against that host count. If the architecture has N hosts, state N and use N × 2.77 PFLOP/s as capacity throughout.
acceptance_test: The mini-case must contain an explicit host count and a capacity calculation that is consistent at both 10 rps and 40 rps. The 18.6× oversubscription figure must be reproducible from the stated host count and per-host capacity.

observed: The text says percentiles are read by linear interpolation on the sorted sample. With N = 10,000 and exactly 100 stragglers at 5.0 s, the p99 rank is approximately 1 + (N−1)×0.99 = 9900.01. Linear interpolation between rank 9900 (1.33 s) and rank 9901 (5.0 s) gives approximately 1.37 s, not 1.33 s.
evidence: 1.33 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.33) = 1.3667 s. The printed p99 ≈ 1.33 s is the nearest-rank or floor value, not the linear-interpolation value.
root_cause: The percentile convention stated in the text does not match the percentile value printed.
correction: Either change the p99 value to ≈1.37 s under linear interpolation, or state that the p99 is computed by nearest-rank/floor convention. Do not say 'linear interpolation' and then print the floor value.
acceptance_test: Recompute p99 from the stated sample and percentile convention. The printed value must match the stated convention within rounding tolerance.

quoted_clause: ≈ 1.5 PFLOP full-square total
observed: The text computes linear prefill FLOPs as ≈1.29 PFLOP, then says the quadratic attention term adds ≈0.2 PFLOP for a ≈1.5 PFLOP full-square total. But the required rate and Table 6-1 use 1.29 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s ≈ 1.19 PFLOPS, not 1.5 PFLOP ÷ 1.08 s ≈ 1.39 PFLOPS.
evidence: 1.5 / 1.08 ≈ 1.39 PFLOPS. The text and table use 1.19 PFLOPS while also presenting 1.5 PFLOP as the full-square total.
root_cause: The chapter mixes linear-only and full-square prefill FLOPs without consistently labeling which one is used in the rate calculation.
correction: Choose one convention and use it consistently. Either use linear-only 1.29 PFLOP throughout and remove the full-square total from the rate discussion, or use the full-square 1.5 PFLOP and update the required rate to ≈1.39 PFLOPS and Table 6-1 accordingly.
acceptance_test: Every prefill FLOP total, required PFLOPS value, and Table 6-1 entry must use the same stated convention. Recompute 1.29/1.08 and 1.5/1.08 and verify that the printed values match the chosen convention.

quoted_clause: high HBM util, low FLOP util
observed: The decode row's resource tell says 'high HBM util', but the same row states '~21–25% achieved HBM util at the canonical point'. 21–25% is not high HBM utilization.
evidence: The table's own number contradicts its resource-tell label. The text also says a decode kernel pinned at ~95% HBM bandwidth is the illustrative bandwidth-bound signature, which is far above 21–25%.
root_cause: The resource-tell column describes a generic bandwidth-bound signature, while the verdict column describes the canonical operating point where HBM utilization is only ~21–25% because the TPOT budget includes other costs.
correction: Either change the resource tell to 'moderate HBM util, low FLOP util' for the canonical point, or explicitly distinguish the generic signature (~95% HBM) from the canonical operating point (~21–25% HBM). Do not label 21–25% as 'high'.
acceptance_test: The resource-tell text for the decode row must be consistent with the utilization number printed in the same row. If the table keeps 'high HBM util', the number must be high; if the number stays 21–25%, the label must be changed or qualified.

quoted_clause: high FLOP / MFU util, mid bandwidth
observed: The prefill row's resource tell says 'high FLOP / MFU util', but the text says the canonical 8×H100 host has aggregate peak ~7.9 PFLOPS and 'comfortably satisfies' the ~1.19 PFLOPS prefill rate. That is ~15% MFU, not high FLOP/MFU utilization.
evidence: 1.19 / 7.9 ≈ 0.15. The table's H100 capacity column is single-device (~0.989 PFLOPS), but the canonical host is 8×H100. The resource tell conflates a single-device roofline illustration with the canonical host's actual utilization.
root_cause: The table mixes single-device capacity comparisons with canonical-host utilization language without distinguishing the two scopes.
correction: Qualify the prefill resource tell as a single-device roofline illustration, or change it to 'compute-regime (intensity above ridge), not necessarily high MFU on the 8-GPU host'. If the table is about the canonical host, use the aggregate 7.9 PFLOPS capacity and state the actual MFU.
acceptance_test: The prefill resource-tell text must be consistent with the capacity basis used in the same row. If the row uses single-device capacity, say so; if it uses the canonical 8×H100 host, the MFU number must match 1.19/7.9 ≈ 15%.

quoted_clause: zeroing goodput
observed: The common-mistakes bullet says bigger batches can 'zero goodput'. The earlier goodput example says the extra tokens can leave goodput 'effectively unchanged' in Scenario A, and Scenario B shows goodput rising from 48 to 65.8. Neither is zero.
evidence: The chapter's own worked example does not support 'zeroing goodput'. A p95 breach can reduce or fail to improve goodput, but it does not necessarily zero it.
root_cause: Overstated claim strength in a summary bullet.
correction: Replace 'zeroing goodput' with 'reducing goodput or preventing it from improving' or similar qualified language.
acceptance_test: The common-mistakes bullet must be consistent with the goodput scenarios in §3. No claim of zero goodput should appear unless a scenario actually computes zero.

quoted_clause: ~20 ms/token
observed: The scope note says the 50→70 tok/s figures are low-batch decode operating points with '~20 ms/token'. 50 tok/s corresponds to 20 ms/token, but 70 tok/s corresponds to ~14.3 ms/token.
evidence: 1 / 50 = 0.020 s = 20 ms. 1 / 70 ≈ 0.0143 s = 14.3 ms. The single '~20 ms/token' label does not apply to both rates.
root_cause: The per-token latency label is attached to a range of throughput values without recomputing per-token latency for the upper value.
correction: State the per-token latency for each rate, or say '~14–20 ms/token' for the 50–70 tok/s range.
acceptance_test: The per-token latency range must be consistent with the stated tokens/s range: 50 tok/s ↔ 20 ms/token, 70 tok/s ↔ ~14.3 ms/token.

page_hint: Chapter 6, §3 Reading Telemetry Into a Decision
quoted_clause: byte-identical shared prefix
observed: Prefix caching operates on token sequences, not raw bytes. 'Byte-identical' is imprecise and can mislead readers into thinking the cache matches raw text bytes rather than tokenized prefixes.
evidence: The chapter elsewhere correctly describes prefix caching as reusing a shared prompt prefix and discusses token counts (1,200-token prompt). The mechanism is token-level KV reuse.
root_cause: Terminology drift between byte-level and token-level descriptions of caching.
correction: Replace 'byte-identical shared prefix' with 'token-identical shared prefix' or 'exact token prefix'.
acceptance_test: Search Chapter 6 for 'byte-identical' in the context of prefix caching. It should be replaced with token-level terminology unless the text is explicitly discussing byte-level storage.

page_hint: Table 7-2 and its note; Fig 7.6 caption
quoted_clause: fine-tuning (QLoRA, 4-bit base + LoRA) | quantized base + LoRA adapters + KV ... the ~24 GB KV that Fig 7.6 lists
observed: The QLoRA fine-tuning row and note include a KV cache in the training memory floor. Fine-tuning does not use an autoregressive KV cache; it uses activations, gradients, optimizer state, and workspace. Including ~24 GB of inference KV overstates the QLoRA training floor and contradicts the chapter's own definition of the fine-tuning floor as weights + gradients + optimizer states.
evidence: The chapter states earlier: 'In fine-tuning, the floor rises further to weights + gradients + optimizer states.' Table 7-2 then lists 'quantized base + LoRA adapters + KV' and the note says the QLoRA floor 'holds ... the ~24 GB KV that Fig 7.6 lists.' That is an inference-state component, not a training-state component.
root_cause: Inference KV residency was carried into the fine-tuning comparison without re-inventorying state by lifetime.
correction: Remove KV from all fine-tuning rows and from the QLoRA note. Replace it with an explicit activation/workspace term or state that activations are excluded from the floor and must be measured. If the book wants to discuss inference after fine-tuning, separate that from the training floor.
acceptance_test: No fine-tuning row or note includes KV cache as a training memory component; the QLoRA floor is derived from 4-bit base + adapters + optimizer + explicitly labeled activation/workspace assumptions.

quoted_clause: When evaluating a model where the hidden dimension or layer count differs from LLaMA-70B, recompute the constant factor
observed: The text uses LLaMA-70B as if it followed the full-MHA formula and had ~2.62 MB/token at FP16. Earlier in the same chapter, LLaMA-2 70B is correctly described as GQA with 64 query heads and 8 KV heads, giving ~0.33 MB/token. The measurement formula is explicitly the full-MHA formula using d_hidden, so it cannot be applied to LLaMA-70B by changing only layer count and hidden dimension.
evidence: The chapter's GQA sensitivity note says: 'LLaMA-2 70B, for instance, has 64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads, so per-token KV shrinks by the head ratio to ... ≈0.33 MB/token.' Measurement point 1 then says 'For a 70B model at FP16 the answer is 2×80×8192×2 B = 2,621,440 B ≈ 2.62 MB/token' and refers to 'LLaMA-70B' as the baseline.
root_cause: The canonical full-MHA teaching geometry and the named LLaMA-70B GQA model were conflated.
correction: Replace 'LLaMA-70B' in measurement point 1 with 'the canonical full-MHA 70B teaching geometry.' State that for any real model the formula is 2 × layers × n_KV-heads × head_dim × bytes, and that LLaMA-2 70B must use 8 KV heads, not hidden_dim.
acceptance_test: No passage implies LLaMA-70B has 2.62 MB/token at FP16; every per-model KV calculation uses n_KV-heads and head_dim, and the canonical full-MHA geometry is labeled as constructed.

quoted_clause: The residency floor is therefore set by weights + KV (+ activations, in fine-tuning)
observed: This sentence omits gradients and optimizer states from the fine-tuning floor, even though the next paragraph correctly says fine-tuning requires weights + gradients + optimizer states. The parenthetical '( + activations, in fine-tuning)' is incomplete and can mislead a reader into thinking activations are the only additional training term.
evidence: The immediately following paragraph: 'In fine-tuning, the floor rises further to weights + gradients + optimizer states, because every parameter update requires its own momentum and velocity vectors (Adam) or per-parameter scaling (LAMB/RMSProp).'
root_cause: Compressed summary sentence dropped the dominant training-state terms.
correction: Rewrite as: 'The residency floor is weights + KV for inference; for fine-tuning it is weights + gradients + optimizer states + activations/workspace.'
acceptance_test: No sentence in the chapter states or implies that fine-tuning residency is only weights + KV + activations.

quoted_clause: at 17.5 concurrent requests a rank reaches ~99.7% of its 80 GB capacity (17.5 + 8 + 54.25 = 79.75 GB) ... Per-rank budget: 17.5 + 54.5 + 8 = 80 GB ≤ 80 GB
observed: The note mixes two KV-per-rank quantities without labeling them: 54.25 GB is 17.5 × the rounded 3.1 GB/request per rank, while 54.5 GB is the full 436/8 KV budget. The 99.7% figure is computed from the rounded 3.1 GB/request; using the chapter's own 24.90368 GB/request gives 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.4768 GB and 79.9768 GB, i.e. ~99.97%, not ~99.7%. The difference is small but the arithmetic is presented as a hard-ceiling check.
evidence: The chapter gives per-request KV per rank as '24.9 ÷ 8 = ~3.1 GB' and later uses 54.25 = 17.5 × 3.1. It also gives '436 ÷ 8 = ~54.5 GB' as the full KV budget per rank. The two are different quantities and should not be interchanged in a capacity check.
root_cause: Rounding 3.11296 GB to 3.1 GB and then using the rounded value in a percentage-of-capacity calculation.
correction: Either use exact values (24.90368/8 = 3.11296 GB; 17.5 × 3.11296 = 54.4768 GB; total 79.9768 GB ≈ 99.97%) or explicitly label 54.25 GB as 'using rounded 3.1 GB/request' and 54.5 GB as 'full KV budget per rank.' Do not present both as if they were the same per-rank KV quantity.
acceptance_test: The per-rank capacity check uses one clearly labeled KV-per-rank value and the percentage follows from that value; no unlabeled 54.25 vs 54.5 swap remains.

quoted_clause: its size depends on the model's layer count, hidden dimension, and the precision chosen for key and value storage
observed: This early sentence names layer count and hidden dimension but omits KV-head count and head dimension. For GQA/MQA models, KV size depends on n_KV-heads × head_dim, not hidden_dim. The chapter later corrects this, but the first definition is incomplete and can seed the exact misconception the chapter later tries to prevent.
evidence: The chapter's own GQA note says per-token KV is 2 × layers × n_KV-heads × head_dim × bytes, and LLaMA-2 70B is ~8× smaller than the full-MHA hidden-dim formula.
root_cause: The opening definition was written for the full-MHA special case and not generalized.
correction: Change to: 'its size depends on layer count, KV-head count, head dimension, and KV precision (equivalently, the KV width per layer).'
acceptance_test: The first definition of KV size includes KV-head count/head dimension or explicitly says it is stating the full-MHA special case.

page_hint: §1 Concept, quantization paragraph; §5 Common Mistakes, KV-quant bullet
quoted_clause: realized savings land between these 2× and 4× reduction factors ... realized savings land between, once block/scale metadata is counted
observed: The phrase 'land between' has no clear referents and is repeated in the Common Mistakes bullet. For 4-bit KV, the raw bound is 4×; metadata reduces the realized reduction below 4×, but the text does not justify 2× as a lower bound. A reader can reasonably ask 'between what and what?' and may infer a guaranteed 2×–4× range that the arithmetic does not establish.
evidence: The sentence contrasts FP8 2× and 4-bit raw 4×, then says realized savings land 'between these 2× and 4× reduction factors.' But the realized 4-bit reduction could be below 2× if metadata/block overhead is large, and the text gives no lower-bound derivation.
root_cause: Compressed prose replaced an explicit inequality with an ambiguous 'between.'
correction: State the bound explicitly: 'For 4-bit KV the raw payload bound is 4×; scale/zero metadata and block layout reduce the realized reduction below 4×. Do not assume a specific realized multiplier without the actual layout.' If a 2× lower bound is intended, derive it or label it as a typical planning assumption.
acceptance_test: The text no longer says 'between' without naming both endpoints and the condition under which the lower bound holds.

quoted_clause: any block-layout/scale-offset metadata overhead is NOT vendor-measured
observed: The intended meaning is that metadata overhead is not included in the 1.31 MB/token figure. 'NOT vendor-measured' is the wrong phrase: the overhead is not measured by the vendor, but the real issue is that it is not included in the accounting. This is a small wording defect but it weakens the precision of the table note.
evidence: The same row says 'raw tensor byte-halving' and the surrounding text says metadata is not included. The phrase 'NOT vendor-measured' does not say 'not included.'
root_cause: Wording slip in a table note.
correction: Replace with: 'block-layout/scale-offset metadata overhead is NOT included in this raw-tensor figure.'
acceptance_test: The table note says the metadata is excluded from the quoted figure, not that it is 'not vendor-measured.'

quoted_clause: the ~500 GB headroom (Ch. 4/7, single-request)
observed: The ~500 GB figure is 640 − 140, i.e. headroom after weights only. For a single request at 9.5K, weights + KV ≈ 165 GB, so the actual single-request headroom is ~475 GB, not ~500 GB. The parenthetical 'single-request' makes the number ambiguous.
evidence: The chapter's own numbers: 640 GB pool, 140 GB weights, 24.9 GB KV at 9.5K. 640 − 140 − 24.9 = 475.1 GB.
root_cause: Headroom after weights was labeled as single-request headroom without subtracting the single-request KV.
correction: Either call it '~500 GB after weights' or use '~475 GB after weights + one 9.5K request's KV.'
acceptance_test: The headroom number is labeled with the exact subtraction it represents.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, 'The 1.08 s budget versus the 35% planning rate' paragraph
quoted_clause: The canonical prefill takes about 1.08 s for 9.2K input tokens (Ch 4)
observed: The sentence states as fact that canonical prefill 'takes about 1.08 s', but 1.08 s is the design *budget* (1.2 s TTFT minus ~120 ms retrieval), not a measured or derived prefill time. The very next sentence correctly calls it 'the end-to-end prefill budget'. At the chapter's own 35% MFU planning rate, prefill would take ~0.465 s, not 1.08 s.
evidence: 1.288 PFLOP ÷ (8 × 346 TFLOPS) = 0.465 s at 35% MFU. The 1.08 s figure is 1.2 s − 0.12 s retrieval, i.e. a budget allocation, not a measured duration. The text itself says '1.08 s is the end-to-end prefill budget inside the 1.2 s TTFT'.
root_cause: Wording conflates a design budget with a measured/derived time, creating a false impression that the canonical prefill actually consumes the full 1.08 s.
correction: Replace 'The canonical prefill takes about 1.08 s' with 'The canonical prefill budget is 1.08 s' or 'If prefill consumes the full 1.08 s budget, that implies ~15% MFU'. Keep the subsequent clarification.
acceptance_test: The sentence no longer asserts a measured prefill time; the 15% MFU is explicitly framed as the rate implied by consuming the full budget, not as the actual prefill rate.

quoted_clause: **Attention / memory constrained (within prefill)** — the quadratic attention term, not the linear weights, grows with context
observed: The label says 'Attention / memory constrained', but the explanation is entirely about the quadratic attention *compute* term (4·n_layers·L²·d FLOPs), not about memory bandwidth or capacity. The label conflates attention compute with memory pressure.
evidence: The bullet's own text: 'the quadratic attention term... grows with context; at 128K+ contexts this term dominates prefill cost (at 32K it is already ~+60% — the 4·n_layers·L²·d term)'. This is a FLOP-count argument, not a memory argument.
root_cause: Label drift: 'memory' is carried over from the general prefill/decode discussion but does not describe the actual constraint being diagnosed.
correction: Rename the candidate to 'Attention-compute constrained (within prefill)' or 'Attention-term dominated'. If KV-cache write pressure during prefill is also intended, state it explicitly as a separate sub-case.
acceptance_test: The label matches the explanation: a reader can tell from the label alone that the constraint is attention FLOPs, not memory bandwidth or capacity.

page_hint: Ch 8 §8 mini-case, fourth candidate bullet, final clause
quoted_clause: so the fix is to reduce the attention term (flash-attention, sparse/linear attention), not to batch harder
observed: FlashAttention is listed as a fix for reducing the attention *term* (a FLOP count), but FlashAttention is an I/O-aware kernel that reduces HBM traffic, not attention FLOPs. If the attention term dominates the FLOP count, FlashAttention does not reduce it; sparse/linear attention does.
evidence: FlashAttention reorganizes attention to tile through on-chip memory and cut HBM traffic while preserving the mathematical result (the book's own Ch 15 framing). It does not change the 4·n_layers·L²·d FLOP count. Sparse/linear attention changes the FLOP count.
root_cause: Conflation of two distinct optimizations: reducing attention FLOPs (sparse/linear attention) vs. reducing attention memory traffic (FlashAttention).
correction: Rewrite as: 'the fix is to reduce the attention FLOP term (sparse/linear attention) or, if the attention kernel is memory-bound, to reduce its HBM traffic (FlashAttention)'. Distinguish the two mechanisms explicitly.
acceptance_test: The text no longer implies FlashAttention reduces attention FLOPs; the two optimizations are assigned to their correct resource (FLOPs vs. bytes).

page_hint: Ch 8 §6 Architecture Consequence, third bullet, final sentence
quoted_clause: This is why the H200 represents an inflection point where inference and training hardware lines begin to converge [1P: NVIDIA H200 SXM datasheet].
observed: The claim that H200 is an 'inflection point where inference and training hardware lines begin to converge' is a strong editorial interpretation not supported by the cited datasheet, which documents specifications, not market-positioning or architectural-convergence claims. H200 is H100 with more/faster HBM3e; it is not a new architecture.
evidence: The datasheet cited is a specifications document. The 'inflection point' framing is the author's interpretation, not a first-party claim. The preceding arithmetic (lower ridge due to more bandwidth at similar compute) is correct, but it does not establish an industry-level 'inflection point'.
root_cause: Editorial overreach: a defensible local observation (H200's ridge is lower than H100's) is inflated into a broad industry claim.
correction: Either remove the 'inflection point' sentence or reframe it as a scoped observation: 'H200's lower ridge means some workloads that are memory-bound on H100 become compute-bound on H200 — a reminder that the ridge is a hardware property, not a workload property.' If the convergence claim is retained, cite a source that actually makes it.
acceptance_test: The sentence either is removed or is supported by a source that explicitly makes the convergence claim; the local arithmetic observation is preserved without the unsupported industry framing.

page_hint: Ch 8 §6 Architecture Consequence, second bullet, final clause
quoted_clause: while decode's bandwidth demand is served by wide-memory GPUs or even CPU offload
observed: 'or even CPU offload' is a hand-wavy claim. CPU decode is dramatically slower and viable only for very low-throughput or latency-tolerant scenarios; presenting it as a peer option alongside wide-memory GPUs overstates its practicality.
evidence: CPU decode throughput is typically orders of magnitude below GPU decode for 70B-class models; it is not a general-purpose alternative for the canonical 10–40 rps workload.
root_cause: Compression of a nuanced trade-off into a two-word aside.
correction: Either remove 'or even CPU offload' or qualify it: 'or, for latency-tolerant or very low-throughput workloads, CPU offload'. Do not present it as a peer option for the canonical scenario.
acceptance_test: The CPU-offload mention is either removed or explicitly scoped to latency-tolerant/low-throughput workloads.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, paragraph beginning '19 / 21 / 22 — the full-utilization compute screens...'
quoted_clause: 19 / 21 / 22 — the full-utilization compute screens for cases (i) / (iii) / (ii) — and their labeled 70% × 95% + N−1 policy totals, Ch 16/17: case (i) compute screen 19 → 29 and fleet 21 → 32, case (iii) 21 → 32, case (ii) 22 → 34, KV-only 21 → 32 (the ρ = 1 u-only screen reads 30 / 32 — ceil(N ÷ 0.7) for KV-only 21 and case (ii) 22)
observed: This is a single ~90-word sentence packing six host-count pairs, two policy formulas, and a parenthetical sub-screen. The arithmetic checks out, but the sentence is very hard to parse on first reading.
evidence: The sentence contains: three FLOP cases, three compute-screen values, three policy-total values, a KV-only case, a ρ=1 sub-screen, and a formula — all in one sentence.
root_cause: Information density exceeds what a single sentence can carry without losing the reader.
correction: Split into a short table or a bulleted list: one line per case (i)/(iii)/(ii)/KV-only, each showing compute screen → policy total. Keep the prose to a one-sentence summary ('the screens cluster at 19–22 full-utilization and 29–34 under policy').
acceptance_test: A reader can extract the six host-count pairs without re-reading the sentence more than once; the values are presented in a scannable structure.

page_hint: Ch 8 Table 8-1, 'prefill throughput per GPU' row
quoted_clause: prefill throughput per GPU | ~2,471 tokens/s | 346 TFLOPS ÷ 140 GFLOP/token [DERIVED; **per-GPU scope**]
observed: The throughput is derived from the linear-only 140 GFLOP/token, but the row does not say 'linear only'. A reader could mistake it for the full per-token cost including attention (~164 GFLOP/token at 9.2K), which would give ~2,110 tokens/s.
evidence: The prefill FLOP rows above it are explicitly labeled 'linear only' / 'full-square' / 'causal-triangle', but the throughput row is not. The 140 GFLOP/token is the linear term; the full per-token cost at 9.2K is ~164 GFLOP/token.
root_cause: Labeling inconsistency within the same table: the FLOP rows carry the case label, the throughput row does not.
correction: Add 'linear-only case (i)' to the throughput row's derivation cell, or add a footnote: 'throughput uses the linear-only 140 GFLOP/token; including attention at 9.2K gives ~2,110 tokens/s'.
acceptance_test: The throughput row's scope (linear-only vs. full per-token) is unambiguous from the table alone.

quoted_clause: §1–§3 build the core arithmetic (FLOPs per token, prefill PFLOP counts, H100 sustained utilization) and the roofline that explains why prefill is compute-bound while decode is memory-bound
observed: The roadmap says §1–§3 build 'the core arithmetic', but §2 is titled 'Mental Model' and is conceptual (the trip/ridge analogy, the resource-hierarchy figure), not arithmetic. The parenthetical does mention the roofline, but the framing '§1–§3 build the core arithmetic' is imprecise.
evidence: Section headers: §1 Concept, §2 Mental Model, §3 Worked Example. §2 contains no arithmetic.
root_cause: Roadmap written from memory of the section contents rather than from the section titles.
correction: Reword to '§1–§3 establish the concept, mental model, and worked arithmetic (FLOPs per token, prefill PFLOP counts, H100 sustained utilization) and the roofline...'.
acceptance_test: The roadmap's description of §1–§3 matches the actual section titles and contents.

page_hint: Ch 8 §3, 'Scope note on the single-device roofline here' paragraph
quoted_clause: each GPU streams only its own shard (~0.70 TB/s against its own ~3.35 TB/s, Ch 6)
observed: The phrase '~0.70 TB/s against its own ~3.35 TB/s' is cryptic: it is unclear whether 0.70 TB/s is a demand, a rate, or a comparison. The intended meaning (per-GPU weight-stream demand vs. per-GPU HBM bandwidth) requires the reader to reconstruct the arithmetic.
evidence: 140 GB / 8 GPUs = 17.5 GB per GPU per token; at ~25 ms TPOT, demand ≈ 0.70 TB/s. The text does not show this derivation.
root_cause: Compression of a two-step derivation into a parenthetical.
correction: Expand to: 'each GPU streams only its own ~17.5 GB shard, demanding ~0.70 TB/s of its ~3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth at the canonical TPOT — well within the per-GPU ceiling'.
acceptance_test: A reader can see what 0.70 TB/s represents (per-GPU demand) and why it is compared to 3.35 TB/s (per-GPU capacity) without reconstructing the arithmetic.
